The ancient Greek poet traditionally credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, the two epics that stand at the start of Greek literature. He probably lived in the 8th or early 7th century BCE, but almost nothing certain is known about him, and whether he existed at all is debated.

Later Greeks pictured him as a blind singer from Ionia, the Greek coast of Asia Minor, and several cities claimed him, Smyrna and the island of Chios among them. The ancient lives of Homer are legends.

The poems:

  • The Iliad tells of a few weeks in the tenth year of the Greek siege of Troy, and the anger of the hero Achilles.
  • The Odyssey follows Odysseus on his ten-year journey home from Troy to Ithaca.

Both look back to a heroic age set in the time of Mycenaean Greece, centuries before they were written.

The "Homeric question" asks how they came to be. In the 1930s Milman Parry showed, by studying singers in Yugoslavia, that the poems carry the marks of oral poetry, built from stock phrases like "rosy-fingered dawn" that helped bards compose as they sang. Many scholars now think the epics grew from a long tradition of oral song and were fixed in writing soon after the Greeks took up the alphabet, perhaps by one or two great poets.

The Greeks learned to read from Homer, quoted him as a guide to the gods and to how to live, and argued with him, as Plato did. Through Rome and later Europe, his stories of war and homecoming became part of world literature.
